lesson.title: State, Plan, Do, Conclude: The Complete Inference Framework
lesson.summary: Walks through the full four-step inference framework end to end with a realistic worked example, tying together hypothesis writing, condition checking, calculation, and precise conclusions.
lesson.body:
The four-step process is the whole course's inference machinery organized into one routine you can reuse on any problem. State what you want to estimate or test, in the actual context of the problem, as a parameter or a pair of hypotheses. Plan which procedure fits that goal, and check whether the conditions that procedure requires actually hold. Do the arithmetic, by hand or with technology, to get a test statistic and p-value, or an interval. Conclude by turning that number back into a sentence answering the original question, using the precise interpretation language from communicating results.

Each step earns its place for a reason beyond just organizing an answer. State forces you to pin down the parameter of interest before you touch a formula, which prevents the common error of running a procedure that does not match the question. Plan is where most of the actual statistical reasoning happens, since naming the wrong procedure, or naming the right one but skipping a required condition, random, independent, normal or large sample, invalidates everything that follows no matter how clean the later arithmetic is. Do is mostly mechanical once Plan is right, this is the step a calculator or software is built to handle. Conclude is where a bare number turns into an actual answer to somebody's real question, in context, with honest uncertainty attached.

Here is a complete example. A consumer testing lab wants to know whether two smartphone brands, Brand A and Brand B, differ in true mean battery life under continuous use.

State: Let mu sub A and mu sub B be the true mean battery life, in hours, of all Brand A and all Brand B phones respectively. The hypotheses are H0: mu sub A minus mu sub B equals 0, and Ha: mu sub A minus mu sub B does not equal 0. The lab sets its significance level at alpha equals 0.05 before collecting data.

Plan: This calls for a two-sample t-test for a difference in means, since two independent groups are being compared using their sample means, not a single sample against a fixed value and not paired measurements on the same units. Conditions: Random, independent random samples of 35 Brand A phones and 40 Brand B phones were selected for testing. Independent, the two samples were chosen independently of each other, and each sample is well under 10 percent of all phones of that brand ever manufactured, so sampling without replacement does not meaningfully affect independence within each group. Normal or large sample, both sample sizes are at least 30, 35 and 40, so by the Central Limit Theorem the sampling distribution of the difference in sample means is approximately normal, and t procedures are appropriate even without knowing the shape of the population of battery lives.

Do: The lab records Brand A with a sample mean of 11.2 hours and standard deviation 1.8 hours, and Brand B with a sample mean of 10.5 hours and standard deviation 2.1 hours. The standard error of the difference in means is the square root of, 1.8 squared over 35, plus 2.1 squared over 40, which comes out to about 0.45 hours. The test statistic is t equals, 11.2 minus 10.5 minus 0, divided by 0.45, which is about 1.55. Using technology to find the degrees of freedom gives approximately 73, and the two-sided p-value that corresponds to a t of 1.55 on 73 degrees of freedom is approximately 0.12.

Conclude: Because the p-value of about 0.12 is greater than alpha equals 0.05, the lab fails to reject H0. There is not convincing evidence of a difference in true mean battery life between Brand A and Brand B phones. It is worth pairing this with a confidence interval for mu sub A minus mu sub B to show the plausible size of any real difference, and worth remembering that failing to reject H0 never proves the means are equal, it only means this sample did not supply strong enough evidence of a difference. A larger sample might have shrunk the standard error enough to detect a real but modest gap, the sample size impact from earlier in this unit, and if the phones tested were not truly randomly and independently sampled, the conclusion's scope would be limited in exactly the way the study limitations section describes.

This same skeleton works unchanged whether the actual procedure is a one-proportion z-test, a chi-square test for independence, or inference for a regression slope. Only State and Plan change to match the specific procedure, Do and Conclude follow the same shape every time. That consistency is exactly why this framework can be graded on a consistent rubric, and why it is worth over-learning as a habit rather than reconstructing from scratch on every problem.
